stem:
At a GP shared-care booking visit at ten weeks, a 29-year-old is found to be rubella non-immune. She has no rash or known exposure. She plans to breastfeed, and she asks when she should be vaccinated.

What should the GP advise?

options.label: A
options.text: MMR now, as the live-vaccine risk to the fetus is theoretical
options.explanation: Inadvertent vaccination in pregnancy has not been shown to harm the fetus, so it is not a reason to end a pregnancy. MMR is still a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy, so it is not given at a booking visit.

options.label: B
options.text: MMR at 28 weeks, once fetal organ formation is complete
options.explanation: MMR is contraindicated at any gestation, not only during organ formation.

options.label: C
options.text: MMR after the birth, once breastfeeding has finished
options.explanation: Breastfeeding is not a contraindication to MMR. Waiting until weaning leaves her non-immune going into a future pregnancy.

options.label: D
options.text: MMR after the birth, before she leaves the maternity unit
options.explanation: MMR is a live vaccine and waits until after the birth. Giving it before discharge, while she breastfeeds, closes the gap before the next pregnancy; she then avoids pregnancy for 28 days.

options.label: E
options.text: Normal human immunoglobulin now, with MMR after the birth
options.explanation: Immunoglobulin is not given to a non-immune woman without an exposure, and it would not give lasting immunity.

context: A rubella non-immune pregnant woman has MMR after the birth, ideally before maternity discharge; breastfeeding is not a reason to delay.
